Midianites
MID-ee-un-ites
n. pl.
From Midian, the fourth son of Abraham by Keturah (Genesis 25:2), whose descendants ranged the deserts east and south of the Gulf of Aqaba. Webster 1828 has no separate entry; the Authorized Version uses the form some sixty times, and the King James translators keep the older spelling Midianitish for the adjective in Numbers 25:6.

Biblical Definition

The Midianites are Abraham’s children by Keturah, and therefore Israel’s distant kin — which makes their history the more sobering. They are first seen as caravan traders who carry Joseph down into Egypt (Genesis 37:28, 36). Moses marries into them, and his father in law Jethro, priest of Midian, gives him the wisest civil counsel in the Pentateuch. Yet the same nation supplies the most successful assault ever made on Israel, and it was not made with the sword. At Shittim the daughters of Moab and Midian drew Israel into the sacrifices of their gods, and Israel joined himself unto Baalpeor (Numbers 25:3), and twenty and four thousand died of the plague. The LORD’s verdict names the method exactly: Vex the Midianites, and smite them: for they vex you with their wiles (Numbers 25:17-18). Wiles, not weapons. In the days of the judges Midian returns as a locust host with the Amalekites and the children of the east (Judges 6:33), and God breaks them with three hundred men and empty pitchers, having first stripped Gideon’s army down expressly lest Israel vaunt themselves against me (Judges 7:2). Isaiah remembers that night as the pattern of deliverance: the day of Midian.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 has no MIDIANITE entry, the lexicon being sparing with biblical gentilics; the sense is fixed entirely by the Authorized Version’s consistent usage from Genesis 37 to Isaiah 10.

expand to see more

MIDIANITE, n. — A descendant of Midian, the son of Abraham by Keturah; one of the nomadic peoples of the Arabian desert east of the Red Sea.

Webster 1828 does not carry the word; the definition here follows the Authorized Version’s usage, which is uniform.

The adjective Midianitish appears in Numbers 25:6, 14, 15, 18 — an older English formation the King James translators preserved.

Isaiah 9:4 and 10:26 use the day of Midian as a byword for a deliverance God alone accomplished.

Where a gentilic is missing from 1828, the King James Version’s own steady rendering supplies the working definition.

Key Scripture

Genesis 37:28 — "Then there passed by Midianites merchantmen; and they drew and lifted up Joseph out of the pit, and sold Joseph to the Ishmeelites for twenty pieces of silver: and they brought Joseph into Egypt."

Numbers 25:3 — "And Israel joined himself unto Baalpeor: and the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel."

Numbers 25:18 — "For they vex you with their wiles, wherewith they have beguiled you in the matter of Peor, and in the matter of Cozbi, the daughter of a prince of Midian, their sister, which was slain in the day of the plague for Peor’s sake."

Judges 6:33 — "Then all the Midianites and the Amalekites and the children of the east were gathered together, and went over, and pitched in the valley of Jezreel."

Judges 7:2 — "And the LORD said unto Gideon, The people that are with thee are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hands, lest Israel vaunt themselves against me, saying, Mine own hand hath saved me."

Modern Corruption

The lesson of Midian is corrupted whenever the church expects the enemy to come as an enemy. Peor teaches that the assault which actually succeeds arrives as hospitality, a feast, and a marriage, not as an army.

expand to see more

Balaam could not curse Israel; Numbers 22 through 24 is four failed attempts and four blessings. So the counsel of Balaam, which Numbers 31:16 and Revelation 2:14 both name explicitly, changed the weapon. What no imprecation could do, an invitation did. The daughters of Moab and Midian called Israel to a feast, and the feast was to the gods, and the men who had crossed the Red Sea dry-shod bowed down. This is the single most instructive military fact in the Pentateuch, and the church has spent twenty centuries relearning it. Persecution has never emptied a congregation the way a comfortable alliance with the surrounding religion has.

The second corruption is the modern reading of Gideon’s three hundred as a leadership parable about elite teams and lean organizations. Judges 7:2 forecloses that reading in advance: the army was reduced lest Israel vaunt themselves against me. The reduction was not tactical wisdom; it was the removal of every ground of boasting, so that the victory could be attributed to no one but God. Every retelling that makes the three hundred a study in excellence has inverted the text. The pitchers were empty and the trumpets were not weapons. The sword of the LORD, and of Gideon — and in that order.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Midyan (H4080), Midian, from a root din meaning strife or judgment; Midyani (H4084) is the gentilic.

expand to see more

Hebrew Midyan (H4080) — Midian; son of Abraham by Keturah (Genesis 25:2) and the land of his descendants.

Hebrew Midyani (H4084) — Midianite; the gentilic used through Numbers, Judges, and Isaiah.

Hebrew nekel (H5231) — wile, craft, subtlety; the word behind they vex you with their wiles (Numbers 25:18).

Hebrew Ba’al Pe’or (H1187) — Baalpeor, the lord of Peor, the Moabite-Midianite deity of Numbers 25:3.

Genesis 37 calls the traders both Midianites and Ishmeelites; the terms overlap for the desert caravan peoples descended from Abraham.

Usage

"They vex you with their wiles (Numbers 25:18) — the divine verdict on how Midian actually fought."

"Lest Israel vaunt themselves against me (Judges 7:2) — why the army was made small."

"Midianites merchantmen (Genesis 37:28) — the caravan that carried Joseph, and providence, down into Egypt."
